slides.title: Fair questions, unfair tests
slides.text: Step 3.3 taught fair questions. But a fair question can still get an unfair answer if the test only reaches one kind of person.
slides.alt: The recess app testers grouped by grade: one single bar, Grade 3. No other grade tried the app.

focus.cue: Grouped by grade: one bar only

slides.title: Who is missing?
slides.text: A sample leaves people out when it only reaches one grade, one lunch line or one kind of voice. The data then speaks for that group, not for everyone.
slides.alt: The lunch vote sorted by Voted: every No is a veggie eater. The screen stood in the meat line.

focus.cue: Sorted by Voted: the No rows
All veggie eaters: they were never asked

slides.title: Compare percents, not counts
slides.text: A voice helper worked for 9 of 10 deep voices and 3 of 6 high voices. The counts say 9 against 3. Percents tell the fair story.
steps: the helper works far better for deep voices
slides.alt: The voice helper: worked for 9 of 10 deep voices (90%) and 3 of 6 high voices (50%).

slides.text: Good technology works for everyone: every grade, every voice, every kind of eyesight. Designers test with many kinds of people, then fix what the test finds.
slides.title: Test it on everyone

words.means: a test tried by every kind of person who will use the thing
never asked or never tested, so the data misses you
designing so everyone can use a thing, whatever their body or voice is like
a person who tries a thing so designers can see if it works for them
